title: An exact positive-series formula for cumulative native wage losses
scope: Infinite-horizon discounted earnings loss in the source's homogeneous-labor capital-adjustment benchmark.
significance: Derives an exact convergent positive series and certified second-order approximation, distinguishing impact share from adjustment speed without a simulated calibration.
body:
# Exact cumulative wage losses with capital adjustment

The source bounds the cumulative native wage loss between two geometric sums. Its exact wage path permits a sharper representation: cumulative losses are an explicitly convergent positive series, with a controlled second-order approximation. This quantifies transition losses even when wages eventually recover completely.

Use \(x=M/(N+M)\in[0,1)\), \(r=1-\eta\in[0,1)\), baseline wage \(\bar w>0\), and \(0<\alpha<1\). For any \(0<\beta\le1\), define the infinite-horizon loss
\[
\mathcal L=\bar w\sum_{t=0}^\infty\beta^t
              \{1-(1-xr^t)^\alpha\}.
\tag{A}
\]
It is finite by the source's upper bound, since \(\beta r<1\). The case \(x=0\) gives zero.

For \(k\ge1\), let
\[
c_k=(-1)^{k+1}{\alpha\choose k}.
\]
Every \(c_k\) is positive: for \(k\ge2\), the product defining the binomial coefficient has one positive factor and \(k-1\) negative factors. The binomial expansion on \(0\le z<1\) therefore gives
\[
1-(1-z)^\alpha=\sum_{k=1}^\infty c_kz^k.
\]
Substitute \(z=xr^t\) into (A). All terms are nonnegative, so exchanging the sums is justified by monotone convergence, without assuming absolute convergence in advance. Summing each geometric series yields the exact identity
\[
\frac{\mathcal L}{\bar w}
=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{c_kx^k}{1-\beta r^k}.
\tag{B}
\]
Its finiteness follows independently from the upper bound on (A). Thus partial sums of (B) are certified lower bounds on the actual loss.

The first two terms give
\[
\frac{\mathcal L}{\bar w}
=\frac{\alpha x}{1-\beta r}
+\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)x^2}{2(1-\beta r^2)}
+\mathcal R.
\tag{C}
\]
The remainder has the explicit bound
\[
0\le\mathcal R\le
\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)(2-\alpha)x^3(1-x)^{\alpha-3}}
     {6(1-\beta r^3)}.
\tag{D}
\]
To verify it, differentiate \(f(z)=1-(1-z)^\alpha\) three times:
\(f'''(z)=\alpha(1-\alpha)(2-\alpha)(1-z)^{\alpha-3}\).
On \([0,x]\) this derivative is positive and bounded above by its value at \(x\). Taylor's integral remainder is therefore between zero and that bound times \(z^3/6\). Apply it at \(z=xr^t\) and sum. This proves (D), rather than treating the second-order expansion as an unqualified numerical approximation.

Every term in (B) increases with \(x\) and with \(r\). For a positive inflow, cumulative losses therefore rise strictly as adjustment slows, apart from a boundary comparison with no change in \(r\). This statement holds at \(\beta=1\); eventual recovery does not imply zero undiscounted transition losses. The first two denominators also distinguish first-order propagation \(r\) from second-order propagation \(r^2\).

Boundary checks are exact. If \(\eta=1\), then \(r=0\), and (B) reduces to \(\sum_kc_kx^k=1-(1-x)^\alpha\), the impact-period loss alone. If \(M=0\), every term vanishes. As \(\eta\downarrow0\) with \(\beta=1\) and \(x>0\), even the first term diverges; the limit approaches a nonadjusting capital stock and is different from every fixed positive adjustment rate.

This is a mathematical refinement of the announced capital-adjustment technology. It does not derive that technology from saving behavior, combine renter losses with native ownership gains, or identify migration selection and innovation responses. No simulated or empirical result is claimed.

title: The exact joint transport-sensitivity region for four Shapley mechanisms
scope: Joint sensitivity of the four education mechanism allocations to independently bounded modular-intervention mean shifts.
significance: Derives a sharp zonotope and support formula, incorporates efficiency dependence, and improves the coordinate radius from 2delta to 3delta/2 when endpoint means are fixed.
body:
# Exact joint transport sensitivity of Shapley mechanisms

The manuscript correctly states that coordinate transport bounds need not describe the joint mechanism set. Under its independently bounded intervention-mean shifts, that joint set can be characterized exactly as a finite zonotope. Fixing the endpoint means additionally tightens the coordinate sensitivity bound.

Let \(K\) have four mechanisms and write the Shapley map as \(\phi=Av\), where columns correspond to subsets \(S\subseteq K\). Its coefficients are
\[
A_{kS}=
\begin{cases}
(|S|-1)!(4-|S|)!/4!,&k\in S,\\
-|S|!(3-|S|)!/4!,&k\notin S.
\end{cases}
\tag{A}
\]
Only applicable branches are used, so no negative factorial occurs. This follows directly by collecting each \(v(S)\) in the source's predecessor-set formula.

Suppose the target-minus-source conditional mean shifts obey
\[
|d_S(x)|\le\delta_S(x)
\]
under the target covariate law. Assume these shifts may vary independently across subsets, with no additional monotonicity or common structural restriction, and that the bounds are integrable. Put \(\bar\delta_S=E_T\delta_S(X)\). The exact joint region for the mean mechanism error \(e\) is
\[
\mathcal E=
\left\{Az:|z_S|\le\bar\delta_S\text{ for all }S\right\}.
\tag{B}
\]
Necessity follows by integrating each bounded shift and using linearity of the fixed Shapley map. For sufficiency, any \(z_S\) in the displayed interval can be realized by
\(d_S(x)=z_S\delta_S(x)/\bar\delta_S\) when \(\bar\delta_S>0\), and zero otherwise. These choices satisfy every bound simultaneously and have the desired means. This proves sharpness for the declared mean-function uncertainty class.

For a direction \(t\in\mathbb R^4\), the exact support function is
\[
h_{\mathcal E}(t)=
\sum_{S\subseteq K}\bar\delta_S
\left|\sum_kt_kA_{kS}\right|.
\tag{C}
\]
Each box coordinate maximizes its own linear term by choosing the matching sign. Hence (C) supplies sharp bounds on every linear combination of mechanism errors, not merely four separate intervals. The entire compact convex region is the intersection of the corresponding supporting halfspaces.

Efficiency appears explicitly. Summing (A) across mechanisms gives column sum zero for each intermediate subset, minus one for the empty subset, and plus one for the full subset. Thus
\[
\sum_ke_k=z_K-z_\varnothing.
\tag{D}
\]
If the source and target endpoint means are known to agree, set both endpoint shift bounds to zero. Every admissible error vector then lies on the three-dimensional efficiency hyperplane \(\sum_ke_k=0\). Choosing separate coordinate extrema that do not sum to zero is impossible.

For a common bound \(\delta\) on every intervention mean, the coordinate support radius is the source's \(2\delta\), because the positive and negative Shapley weights each sum to one. If the two endpoint means are fixed and only intermediate shifts have that bound, each coordinate radius improves to
\[
\delta\sum_{S\ne\varnothing,K}|A_{kS}|=3\delta/2.
\]
The removed empty and full columns each had absolute coefficient \(1/4\). This improved radius is sharp individually: choose each allowed shift with the sign of its coefficient in row \(k\). Those choices generally do not attain the other coordinates' extrema simultaneously, precisely as (B) records.

This result formalizes joint uncertainty for well-defined modular interventions. If the mean functions must also obey monotonicity, outcome-range limits or a shared structural parameter, the box in (B) must be intersected with those restrictions before mapping it; (B) is then only an outer region. It does not make schooling randomization identify unobserved mechanism interventions, or establish population overlap and invariance empirically.

title: Rich endpoint distributions can identify the sign of controlled ownership effects
scope: Sharp distribution-informed missing ownership-scale cell bounds under the source's individual monotonicity and Lipschitz scale restriction.
significance: Completes the source's richer-data suggestion with an exact joint rectangle and a binary-endpoint example where distributions establish positive controlled effects although means alone do not.
body:
# Endpoint distributions can identify controlled-effect signs

The source carefully distinguishes its sharp mean-data bounds from what richer endpoint distributions imply. Under its individual scale restriction, the distribution-informed bounds can be completed exactly, including the joint set of both controlled ownership effects.

Write \(A_0=A(0,s_0)\) and \(A_1=A(1,s_1)\), with identified marginal distributions on \([0,1]\), means \(a,b\), and \(c=L(s_1-s_0)\ge0\). The missing cells are \(B_0=A(0,s_1)\) and \(B_1=A(1,s_0)\). The source's individual restriction gives
\[
A_0\le B_0\le\min(1,A_0+c),\qquad
\max(0,A_1-c)\le B_1\le A_1.
\tag{A}
\]
Define
\[
u_0=E[\min(1,A_0+c)],\qquad
l_1=E[\max(0,A_1-c)].
\]
Then the exact joint mean set of missing cells is
\[
(E B_1,E B_0)\in[l_1,b]\times[a,u_0].
\tag{B}
\]
Consequently the exact joint set of controlled ownership effects is
\[
(\tau_F(s_0),\tau_F(s_1))
\in[l_1-a,b-a]\times[b-u_0,b-a].
\tag{C}
\]

To prove sharpness, couple the observed endpoint variables \(A_0,A_1\) arbitrarily; their joint cross-regime distribution is not observed or restricted. For any constants \(\lambda_0,\lambda_1\in[0,1]\), set
\[
B_0=A_0+\lambda_0\{\min(1,A_0+c)-A_0\},
\]
\[
B_1=\max(0,A_1-c)
+\lambda_1\{A_1-\max(0,A_1-c)\}.
\]
These missing outcomes obey (A) pointwise and independently span both mean intervals. Linear interpolation over scale between each ownership-specific pair of endpoints has slope between zero and \(L\), stays in \([0,1]\), and supplies a complete admissible response function. Thus every pair in (B), and hence every pair in (C), is attained while preserving both full observed endpoint distributions. Degenerate intervals cause no difficulty. This proof does not impose an unobserved common-rank coupling.

The controlled interaction \(I=\tau_F(s_1)-\tau_F(s_0)\) therefore has the sharp interval
\[
I\in[a-u_0,\ b-l_1].
\]
Subtracting opposite endpoints of (C) proves inclusion, and the construction above attains both extremes simultaneously. These joint statements require the source's absence of cross-ownership shape restrictions; additional restrictions would couple the two missing cells.

The improvement over mean-only bounds can change a substantive sign conclusion. Take endpoint outcomes to be binary, with \(\Pr(A_0=1)=3/10\), \(\Pr(A_1=1)=3/5\), and \(c=2/5\). Then
\[
l_1=(1-c)b=9/25,\qquad
u_0=a+c(1-a)=29/50.
\]
Equation (C) yields
\[
\tau_F(s_0)\in[3/50,3/10],\qquad
\tau_F(s_1)\in[1/50,3/10].
\]
Both controlled effects are strictly positive throughout the identified set. Using only the same means, the source's intervals are \([-1/10,3/10]\) at both scales, leaving either sign possible.

Why does the difference arise? When a unit's high-scale endpoint is one, the scale restriction forces its low-scale outcome to be at least \(1-c\). When a unit's low-scale endpoint is zero, its high-scale outcome cannot exceed \(c\). Averaging these individual restrictions is stronger than clipping only the mean.

This is a sharp conditional identification refinement. It does not identify actual multinational spillovers, justify an infeasible ownership-scale intervention, or recover physical productivity from revenue data. It retains fixed domestic-firm identities, the specified investment version and exposure mapping, and leaves causal assignment and cohort follow-up requirements intact.
